title: Medical University of Vienna
paragraphs: My dream is to practise medicine in countries with underdeveloped healthcare. When I first aspired to be a doctor, I vaguely liked children and decided to go to medical school because I wanted a job in which I could relieve such children of their suffering and bring their smiles back. However, through volunteering at an orphanage in Cambodia in my third year of university, my dream became more concrete: to save children in developing countries who do not have access to adequate food, medical care, education and so on. The fact that I studied at the Medical University of Vienna through the study abroad program this time may seem at first glance far removed from healthcare in developing countries, but I applied because I thought it would be the first step toward working alongside overseas medical professionals in developing countries in the future.
In my clerkships at the Medical University of Vienna this time, I rotated through cardiology, emergency medicine and family medicine.

In the cardiology clerkship, which began the day after I arrived in Vienna, I was surprised by the differences in medical education between the Medical University of Vienna and Nagoya University. There are about 700 medical students in one year, so naturally the supervising teachers cannot give sufficient attention in hospital clerkships. As a result, the role of medical students was mainly "tasks" that one can do alone, such as blood sampling, securing intravenous lines and connecting infusions. In clerkships in Japan, a supervising teacher is always with you, lectures are provided and you can ask questions at any time, so I was bewildered at first. For example, if I wanted to take the history of a new patient outside of those tasks, I had to find a new patient myself and prepare "perfectly" on my own how to take the history and so on (because there was almost no teaching from the supervising doctors). However, being able to learn that I have to find chances to learn on my own and make use of them was a very big gain. In the ER clerkship, I was allowed to do procedures ordered by doctors such as blood sampling, ECG and securing intravenous lines, as well as to interpret and discuss the results, and I also conducted medical interviews with the occasional patient from a non-German-speaking country. I was able to experience what it means to take part in medical care in English and to see patients in English, which was a very valuable experience. The last clerkship I rotated through was family medicine. Here I was allowed to visit public health-related facilities and to do a visiting clerkship staying overnight at a family doctor's office. In the public health facility visits, I visited a facility supporting people with AIDS, a facility supporting homeless people, a facility for drug addicts and so on. Among them, the one that left the strongest impression on me was the facility for drug addicts, which went to clubs and parties, had the drugs that participants carried analysed, and told users about their dangers. Even if they were carrying illegal drugs, they did not report them; they simply explained the dangers from a medical standpoint. I strongly sympathised with the approach of not simply banning them but helping people recover from within by telling them about the dangers. In the overnight clerkship at the family doctor's home, I of course learned the reality of family medicine in Vienna, and through the home visits I was also able to learn about the state of elderly care in Vienna. Vienna is aging just like Japan, and elderly care is said to be a big topic. What impressed me most was that there were not a few households that employed live-in nurses from abroad. They hired people from poorer neighbouring countries such as Romania and Hungary, who lived in the home and provided around-the-clock nursing.

Although it is not directly related to the exchange program, after the 12 weeks of clerkships at the Medical University of Vienna, I did a four-week clinical clerkship at Angkor Hospital for Children in Cambodia. Because this hospital is supervised by Western doctors, everything, including rounds and charts, is done in English. On the inpatient ward I was in charge of about three to four child patients at all times, and spent each day doing the morning rounds, charting and writing orders all by myself, and finalising the orders after discussion with the supervising doctor. Every other day there were general rounds by an Australian doctor, where I presented my patients, and I was able to do clerkship work of a scope I could not have experienced in Vienna, so my days were very fulfilling. What left the strongest impression on me in the four weeks in Cambodia was a four-year-old child with ALL. Since I had done my clerkship in the Department of Pediatrics at Nagoya University Hospital, I had taken it for granted that chemotherapy is given for pediatric hematologic malignancies. In Cambodia, however, even at Angkor Hospital for Children, where relatively advanced care is provided because it is under Western supervision, chemotherapy was not provided. Moreover, the child sat on the bed with an abdomen so swollen that walking was difficult, not even knowing whether a treatment existed. I was greatly shocked by this scene, and my wish to practise medicine in countries with underdeveloped healthcare was updated into the concrete wish to bring chemotherapy to such countries as a specialist in pediatric hematology and oncology.

Finally, I am deeply grateful to Dr. 粕谷 and the professors of the International Exchange Office, who gave me the valuable opportunity of studying abroad, to the Student Affairs staff, and to Dr. 吉田, who greatly helped by introducing my homestay and in other ways. I will definitely make use of this experience in my future career.
